reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it demonstrates how to fix a Chrome proxy-connection problem by navigating server, proxy, and LAN settings. The Facebook contact address is presented as a communication method and is not connected to a financial offer, payment requirement, credential request, or deceptive participation flow.

citations.quote: Then change the server and the proxy set. Then we go into the LAN set. Then we drop the health tag from here. And we press OK.
Then the problem will not appear with you again.

opening.argument: The video links a viewer action to a promised resolution through an external contact route. It tells viewers to contact the uploader, describes a method for a broken Chrome installation, and then instructs them to alter server, proxy, and LAN settings before asserting that the problem will not appear again. That is more than neutral troubleshooting: it is a low-barrier action-and-outcome funnel whose success cannot be independently established from the material shown. The imperative configuration steps and the invitation to communicate externally make the promised fix dependent on following the promoted route.

citations.quote: To communicate with us http://www.facebook.com/t3leeme The method is available for a broke chrome (Google Chrome)
Then change the server and the proxy set. Then we go into the LAN set. Then we drop the health tag from here. And we press OK.
Then the problem will not appear with you again.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the address a mere communication method does not resolve the linkage. The video presents that external route alongside a purported method and gives configuration steps tied to a categorical outcome. It does not establish that the procedure is reliable, safe, or sufficient, so the apparent technical framing can function as a solicitation to follow an unverifiable fix.

citations.quote: To communicate with us http://www.facebook.com/t3leeme The method is available for a broke chrome (Google Chrome)
Then the problem will not appear with you again.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted material shows troubleshooting, not acquisition of a reward or asset. The description only says, “To communicate with us,” and the spoken instructions concern server, proxy, and LAN settings. Nothing says viewers receive money, a digital asset, or any other reward for contacting anyone or changing settings. The categorical outcome is a technical claim, not evidence of a qualifying scam flow.

citations.quote: To communicate with us http://www.facebook.com/t3leeme
Then we go into the LAN set.

opening.argument: Several risk signals appear together: an external Facebook address, a vaguely described “method,” and instructions to change connection infrastructure and remove a setting. The speaker then promises the problem will not recur, without explaining why these changes are safe or why they should work. The combination encourages viewers to take consequential technical action while relying on an off-platform contact route and an absolute-sounding result. Even without a payment request, that is a suspicious low-friction intervention presented with more certainty than the evidence supports.

citations.quote: To communicate with us http://www.facebook.com/t3leeme The method is available for a broke chrome (Google Chrome)
Then change the server and the proxy set.
Then we drop the health tag from here.
Then the problem will not appear with you again.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The absence of an explicit payment request is not the only concern. The material directs viewers toward an external address and asks them to alter network settings, including dropping a setting, while offering a definitive result. That combination is materially riskier than ordinary explanation because the viewer is asked to trust an unexplained procedure and an external channel.

citations.quote: Then we drop the health tag from here.
Then the problem will not appear with you again.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These are ordinary troubleshooting risk questions, not evidence of a reward or asset-acquisition scam. The footage shows Chrome and network configuration screens, while the narration identifies server, proxy, and LAN settings. The supplied material contains no reward, payment, account-verification, or asset claim. Criticizing the level of technical explanation cannot supply the missing scam mechanism.

The method is available for a broke chrome (Google Chrome)

opening.argument: Although framed as technical help, the presentation also promotes a method and directs viewers to a specific external contact. The wording does not simply explain a general Chrome feature; it says the method is available for a broken Chrome installation, then walks viewers through changes and closes with a promised permanent resolution. That structure steers viewers toward accepting the uploader’s procedure and contact channel rather than evaluating the problem independently. The educational framing therefore functions as promotion of an externally supplied intervention.
